profilePeriod: Reforming minister and prime minister, 1906–1922, with the 1929 public-works programme and explicitly dated earlier/later context.

sources.title: UK Government: David Lloyd George
sources.evidence: Chancellor promoted pensions and land taxation; wartime industrial mobilisation and executive centralisation; elected coalition in 1918, Versailles in 1919, Irish settlement and resignation after coalition broke in 1922.

sources.title: National Library of Wales: People’s Budget and Welfare State
sources.evidence: State pensions, 1909 redistributive budget and 1911 National Insurance legislation establish social protection, rather than replacement of the entire private economy.

sources.title: National Library of Wales: David Lloyd George papers
sources.evidence: Archival institutional biography records early Welsh Home Rule and disestablishment campaigning, pensions, insurance and coalition government.

sources.title: Commons Library: 1918 centenary
sources.evidence: Representation of the People Act expanded voting to all men and some women; unequal female age/property qualifications remained until 1928.

sources.title: National Army Museum: Irish War of Independence
sources.evidence: British government used expanded police, Black and Tans, Auxiliaries, martial law and official reprisals; 1921 truce/treaty led to self-government and partition, not immediate full republican independence.

sources.title: Hansard: Ex-Enemy Aliens
sources.evidence: Home Secretary Shortt described very restricted admission of former enemy nationals, exceptions for British-born wives and children, short stays and refusal of residence to deported enemy aliens. This is coalition policy, not a personal speech by Lloyd George.

sources.title: Hansard: Munitions statement by Lloyd George
sources.evidence: Lloyd George described systematic machinery censuses, expansion of shell output and lower manufacturing costs: concrete support for industrial technology, state coordination and private contracting.

sources.title: Liberal History: Lloyd George biography
sources.evidence: 1911 Agadir warning rejected peace at any price when British vital interests were threatened; 1923 reunification of Liberals against tariffs; later criticism of unemployment policy timidity.

sources.title: Hansard: Safeguarding of Industries
sources.evidence: Lloyd George defended the established free-trade basis of British shipping, cotton, machinery and banking and opposed new tariff proposals. Opponents identified tension with his own 1921 strategic safeguarding legislation.

sources.title: Church in Wales: Disestablishment history
sources.evidence: Institutional church account describes Lloyd George’s nonconformist campaign for disestablishment, with disagreement over disendowment even among dissenters.

sources.title: G. I. T. Machin: Nonconformity and Radicalism
sources.evidence: Documented causes include temperance, religious equality in burials, undenominational education, opposition to tithes and state church privilege. Religious reform does not imply hostility to religion.

sources.title: National Library of Wales: Votes for Women
sources.evidence: Early support for women’s suffrage coexisted with rejection of the 1910 limited franchise proposal as favouring Conservatives. Supports reforming politics but does not establish modern sexual-identity positions.

sources.title: We Can Conquer Unemployment: original book record/preview
sources.evidence: Book credited to David Lloyd George and Liberal Party; programme includes roads, bridges, housing, telephone development and land drainage, demonstrating practical infrastructure modernisation.

sources.title: Peter Sloman: Can we conquer unemployment?
sources.evidence: Research abstract identifies Lloyd George’s pledge for loan-financed public works in 1929 and later Liberal involvement in the orthodox National Government. The abstract alone was used.

sources.title: National Library of Ireland: War memoirs bibliographic record
sources.evidence: Six-volume War memoirs of David Lloyd George, main creator David Lloyd George, London I. Nicholson & Watson, first publication starting 1933; political and wartime leadership memoir.

sources.title: Hansard: Firearms Bill
sources.evidence: Government firearms bill imposed police certificates, good reason and suitability conditions. This is administration-level evidence of regulation, not a personal statement by Lloyd George.

sources.title: National Library of Wales: letter to William George
sources.evidence: His letter describes reluctant entry into war because of Belgium, followed by determination to fight through. This qualifies both absolute pacifist and unconditional militarist readings.

facts: Early Welsh Home Rule campaign; 1920 Irish devolved structures and 1921 negotiated dominion self-government.
1908–1911 national welfare funding and wartime coordination used central capacity.
estrutura.tension: Territorial self-government subject to imperial framework and central fiscal/social responsibilities; no unlimited unilateral secession principle.

facts: 1911 weakening of hereditary Lords veto and 1918 franchise expansion.
1916–1922 executive centralisation operated inside parliamentary coalition; resignation when coalition support ended.
representacao.tension: Broad male franchise and partial female suffrage coexist with executive pragmatism and parliamentary, rather than direct-assembly, democracy.

facts: 1919–1921 coercion in Ireland included martial law, arrests and reprisals.
1920 government firearms licensing required police approval.
poder.tension: Liberal legal tradition and ordinary parliamentary opposition survived; emergency coercion cannot be treated as uniformly libertarian or totalitarian.

facts: 1920 government severely restricted ex-enemy aliens, with specified family exceptions.
Welsh language/national distinctiveness and religious minority equality were central earlier causes.
imigracao.tension: Border control and national loyalty coexist with internal cultural pluralism; immigration law is not direct evidence of a demand to erase all minority customs.

facts: 1914 personal letter justified entering war for Belgium; 1915 munitions expansion followed.
1919 Versailles/League settlement and 1921 Irish negotiation coexisted with military threats.
diplomacia.tension: Negotiation and force both legitimate; no peace at any price and no permanent-war ideology.

facts: Agadir speech in 1911 asserted British vital interests.
1919 peace settlement and 1922 Turkish crisis show imperial projection, while Irish treaty accepted compromise.
intervencao.tension: International institutions did not erase empire, strategic bases or national interest; not an isolationist.

facts: Pensions and insurance (1908–1911), redistributive taxation and land reform.
1915 industrial policy used both state coordination and private producers.
economia.tension: Social liberal mixed economy: rejects both laissez-faire abandonment and general abolition of owners.

facts: 1909 wealth/land taxation and 1915 organised industrial mobilisation.
1929 loan-financed infrastructure programme to reduce unemployment.
controle.tension: Supports intervention for welfare and investment, not universal state planning of every economic decision.

facts: 1925 explicit defence of free trade and criticism of tariff expansion.
1921 safeguarding policy created narrow strategic exceptions, identified in debate.
comercio.tension: Generally free trading but not indifferent to strategic industrial resilience or emergency security.

facts: Nonconformist disestablishment campaign and undenominational education; religious equality.
Earlier temperance and Free Church activism show a positive religious social inheritance.
religiao.tension: Rejects established-church privilege without identifying secular government with abolition of religion.

facts: Women’s suffrage support from early career, 1910 tactical rejection, partial enfranchisement in 1918.
Temperance and nonconformist reforming public morality were documented earlier influences.
moral.tension: Women’s public participation challenges rigid domestic roles; does not establish modern LGBT, abortion or gender-language positions. Such answers are cautious historical extrapolation, never direct attribution.

facts: 1915 machinery census, organised production and technical efficiency.
1929 roads, telephones, housing and land drainage investment.
tecnologia.tension: Industrial modernisation with employment/social aims is not unlimited transhumanism; genetic engineering, climate and AI questions require analogy.

limitations: Modern Brazilian institutions and technologies are interpreted by historical functional analogy, not represented as literal statements.
Moral/biotechnology items have less direct evidence than economy, war, religion and constitutional practice. Absence of a statement is not used to justify N.
Government policies are distinguished from personal quotations, especially aliens and firearms rules.
Book translation searches for Lloyd George / Memórias de guerra / editora did not verify a Brazilian published edition. Original title retained; this is not proof no translation exists.
The saved historical period is retained; later private opinions are not substituted for 1906–1922 government practice.

recommendedMetadata.reason: Existing PT/EN metadata accurately captures welfare reform, wartime mobilisation, imperial power and negotiated Irish self-government; reported to coordinator before answers.

bookDecision.reason: Self-authored political and wartime leadership memoir; the major six-volume account is a stronger representative work than the shorter jointly credited 1929 election programme. First volume 1933; no verified Brazilian title found.
